speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always listen with attention to the Hon. Member because I know that he does much research into his work. When talking to young people, has he ever put to them the idea that the single most important person involved in their future career and where they will work is the student himself or herself? Quite often we do not go the second mile in questioning them. The Hon. Member may have asked a
January 31, 1984

student why he is at school and received the reply, "I do not have a job and it seemed to be a good place to get into the arts course and maybe delay the fact".
Has he gone to the schools to make those kinds of recommendations? We know that to the credit of the provinces there is much assistance given to young people to channel their goals. Fortunately, guidance councillors are no longer teachers who have little to do; we now have well trained guidance councillors. I suggest that one of the best ways to help young people, rather than asking the Government to make more money available for colleges, is to put some responsibility on the young people, to show them that the biggest responsibility lies with them. While there is a lot of help for them, their success requires their own application not only when they are seeking employment but when they are pursuing a degree. It depends on the extent to which they apply themselves.
Has the Hon. Member found some lethargy in that area, because that was my experience from talking to some people? They had not really applied themselves even with the assistance that was available to them from both levels of government.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a difficult question to answer but I want to be fair to the Hon. Member who asked the question. I do not have a lot of experience with students not wanting to apply themselves. I am talking about university students. I do not have the figure at hand with respect to what is the percentage of student fees covering universities, but the historical rule of thumb is approximately one-third. The other two-thirds come from general taxation or general revenues. 1 do not know what that percentage would be right now.
There is no question that the student has a responsibility. I believe that in my comments this afternoon I did not stress that more money was the simple answer. I did not want to make that point in that way. Obviously more money is always a help, but my real concern is to get a growing economy which would enable us to afford some of these programs.
When we look at training for Canada's youth I think the greater problem is not necessarily with students in university or those coming out of university who are highly motivated and looking for meaningful employment-although some of them become underemployed relative to their training-but rather the type of young person who feels that there is no opportunity for him or her. I know it is difficult to generalize, as the question forces me to do, but we are facing a greater challenge with that type of young person who does not want to go to university or feels that he or she cannot. To them, the training institutions or education generally is just not the answer to their immediate problem. 1 think that is an area on which we will have to spend a lot of time. How do we deal with those people who do not see traditional post-secondary education as a partial answer for their future training but want to get into the job market while having limited skills or experience, if either?
As I said, it is not enough to address ourselves to universities and post-secondary educational institutions with which we are
Established Programs Financing generally familiar but rather we should address ourselves to this group of young Canadians to whom I referred. If they do not get into the job market and find meaningful work, at what stage do they get turned off on the economic system and simply say there is no place or room for them? That is as much my concern as are the others identified by the Hon. Member.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate. I must begin by saying that I am surprised that the debate is being carried only by Members on this side. I have been waiting for more explanation from the Government of the rationale behind this Bill.
I want to join my colleagues in saying that I was somewhat surprised when I read the rationale introduced by the Minister in his speech. Since it seemed so slim, I read it again but found that it did not get any thicker.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Members opposite tell me to sit down and just vote on it. I suspect that is exactly the reason why Liberal Members opposite refuse to debate the Bill. They want this Bill to get out of the House of Commons as fast as possible because I think they are ashamed of it. Frankly, when one reads the Bill one realises that they ought to be ashamed of it.
When we were growing up we were taught the simple lesson that a deal is a deal. If an honourable gentleman or lady made an agreement with you and shook your hand, you presumed that the deal was made and that that person could be trusted. We were also taught to make a deal in writing. The provinces and others had the right to believe that the educational institutions had a deal in writing with the federal Government for the five-year period from 1977 to 1982. The federal Government then came along and said that for its purposes it will put a cap on its side of the deal for 1983-84. What does that say about co-operative federalism as practised by the federal Government in Canada? It tells us that it is not federalist and not very co-operative.
Let me reiterate a couple of points that need to be made about this Bill. In fairness to the Minister, he did state with some reality that the federal Government proposes to put more money into post-secondary education in these two fiscal years. That is true. It proposes to give 6 per cent and 5 per cent more than it was giving. Let me refer specifically to the Minister's comments as reported at page 814 of Hansard on January 27. He said:
The purpose of this Bill is to bring certain fiscal transfers to the provinces into conformity with the anti-inflation program-
He continued:
-federal assistance to each province for post-secondary education will be increased by 6 per cent in 1983-84 and by an additional 5 per cent in 1984-85.
What he does not say thereafter is what other programs are proposed to be constrained. The fact of the matter is that one could have some comprehension of the purposes behind this Bill if federal programs in totality were constrained to six and five. Everyone who reads the blue books knows that that is not

January 31, 1984
Established Programs Financing
true. The federal Government is increasing its spending in each of the constraint years by enormous amounts above 6 per cent and 5 per cent. As well, in this Bill which splits health funding from post-secondary education funding, does the Government plan to apply its six and five program to health care funding? It does not, nor should it. It has an agreement with the provinces in which it undertook to apply the traditional formula of the GNP escalator to all of these programs.
I looked at the Minister's words in search of any rationale whatsoever for the application of the six and five program specifically to post-secondary education since it is not being applied to health or other programs, but is was in vain. I found no explanation at all in the Minister's speech. To my knowledge, no Liberal has yet stood in the House to explain why it is Government policy to constrain federal spending on higher education. That is a travesty. It is a travesty of the parliamentary system. Members opposite have an obligation to tell students and those who wish to become students in the educational institutions across this country why it is public policy to reduce the transfer payments in support of those institutions.
What is going to happen? In Ontario, the federal Government is reducing its cash transfers this year alone by some $41 million. I hope that when the Minister of Education for the Province of Ontario is discussing these matters with Ontario students she will remind students in our institutions, as I am sure she will, that one of the reasons the Province of Ontario does not have as much money as it would like to have to spend on higher education is this Bill. In totality, the Bill proposes to cut $380 million in terms of transfers. Why? Because the Government of Canada chooses to say that the chief purpose of public moneys to be spent on educational programs is for the Government to give credit for those expenditures. It cannot get credit directly, so it prefers to transfer those programs to the youth employment fund, spend the transfers that way and take them out of the educational system. That is the simple bald fact. I knew the Minister who introduced the Bill before his incarnation as a Minister. I have great respect for him personally. I do not know what happens when one joins the Liberal Cabinet, but something drastic does. However, in the words of this Minister, having reread them, I sense the Minister knows that words will not cover what is being done. When the Minister introduced the Bill, he said that the first change being made in the Bill is a change in the name. Let me quote the Minister:
The purpose of this change is to clarify the fact that the federal Government contributes huge amounts to the provinces.
If the purpose of changing the name is to get political credit, then let him say so. The Minister covered that up in somewhat more flowery language. I think that is what he was trying to say. He ought to have had the honesty to admit that that is what he was saying. In the end I think we will find on analysis that that is the entire purpose of this Bill.
What does the Minister say when he attempts to deal with the purpose of the Bill. The Minister said some revealing things. On page 815 of Hansard we find these words:
-the federal Government considers from time to time how best to allocate the huge sums which it allocates to the training and education of our young people.
That is an excellent idea, Mr. Speaker. All programs deserve to be reviewed from time to time to see if they can be better used for those for whom they are intended. 1 continue to quote:
For some lime now, the Government has felt that some of the funds which now move through provinces in a totally unconditional fashion might be more effective if they were channelled through more direct programs.
If that is the rationale for the cut, where in this Bill does the Government move more of its funds to more directly controlled programs? Does the Government do that? No, it does not. It simply reduces the funds without dealing with the principle, which the Minister I take it was espousing, behind the Bill.
The Minister went on to say that as a result of that concern, Ministers of the Crown met with provincial Ministers in order to try to resolve some of these problems. The Minister said:
The Minister of Finance accordingly met with the provincial Ministers of Finance in December, 1982 to exchange views on the economic prospects. He indicated that he had been informed by the Secretary of State that some progress was being made in discussions of support for post-secondary education. The Minister of Finance was therefore able to inform provincial Ministers that it might be unnecessary to introduce measures suggested by his predecessor in 1981. He indicated that he would be prepared-
And these words are self-condemning:
-to see the federal support for post-secondary education increased by 6 per cent in 1983 and by a further 5 per cent in 1984. This would bring such transfers into conformity with the anti-inflation six and five program-
I think the Minister will know that I read the whole paragraph. I do not think he can accuse me in any way of trying to excise quotes or take matters out of context. The implication of those words are clear. In 1982 the Government of Canada changed the understanding with regard to the general financing of health and of education. It abolished the revenue guarantee. The revenue guarantee is a technical phrase meaning that the understandings in 1977 under which provinces had tax points transferred to them, with some risk that revenues might not be equal, provided a guarantee that if revenues from those tax points were to fall below those expectations, the revenues would be topped up. That was the revenue guarantee. The Government abolished that in 1982.
Interestingly enough, the Minister goes on to argue, and this is in parenthesis and I will want to return to it, the validity of calculating the cash payments that are paid to provinces for post-secondary education on the basis that the provinces continue in effect to receive revenues equivalent to the tax points in 1975, 1976 and 1977. The Minister knows that is not true. Precisely because it is not true, the revenue guarantee was abolished in order to save the federal Government money to which it had committed itself years ago. The words are damning. What this Government is saying to the provinces, which have the constitutional responsibility for post-secondary education, is that "No matter what deal we said we would agree to for five years, you have no assurance that we will
January 31, 1984

honour our side of that arrangement during that five-year period." It was one thing in 1982 for the Government to abandon its position with regard to the revenue guarantee. It could at that time at least argue that the original five-year period was up, that a new five-year period was beginning, and therefore the Government had some rights to change the agreement. Whether the Government in fact has the moral right to do so unilaterally is a moot point and a point we debated at length at that time. But there can surely be no question that the Government of Canada has no right to make an arrangement with the provinces of Canada, to say it will live with that arrangement for five years and then change it unilaterally. Surely that is a simple matter of federalism, in other words, the ability to trust an undertaking received from the federal Government that has been put through the House of Commons in a piece of legislation.
I repeat that there might be some justification if, in fact, six and five were being applied to every program of Government, but it is not. It is, as a rule, only being applied to those programs that transfer money to those who need it, whether they are pensioners, educational institutions, or others. The federal Government's main spending programs go on. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether you think in fact, that a large budget is being created right now to sell the Government's upcoming budget proposals? I ask you whether or not the Government has cut back its advertising programs in line with six and five? I ask you whether the Government has cut back on the programs of selling itself to live within the six and five guidelines? The blue books are clear on that one. No way, not the Liberal Government. What will be the effect? One of the ironies is that the Government is not saying that in its view too much money is going into post-secondary education. That is not even its rationale. If you look at the proposal, Mr. Speaker, its rationale is to restrain spending on post-secondary education for two years to six and five. Then it is to return to the agreed formula, recognizing that the application of the six and five will reduce the base upon which the real formula then works. The Government is not arguing that the formula is too generous. It is not arguing that the old base is too generous. It is simply saying that it will stick the six and five on it for political reasons.
The effect is that it will make it more and more difficult for provincial governments to meet the demand of young people who know what a big, tough world they are facing and who want training of whatever kind today to help prepare them. That is the tragedy.
Actually the tragedy is twofold. Other Members of the House have dealt at length with what it will do to our student population. By concentrating on the federal-provincial issue, I do not want to suggest that I feel anything but immense sympathy for the students who will be affected. The Minister should have the courage to take his words and boil them down to what they actually say. At the end of his speech introducing the Bill, he talked about how much the federal Government was doing for young people. He referred to the student loans
Established Programs Financing program, a good program, and to research grants. Others talked about what the Government has done to the Social Sciences Research Council. It has cut them off, in effect. His chief example was: "The Speech from the Throne announced the establishment of the $1 billion youth opportunity fund". Well, here it is, here it is!
If one is young and concerned for his future in the country and knows that he needs to be trained for what is coming, he should not look to the Government to deal co-operatively with the provinces or to use national resources at both levels to achieve purposes which will be of benefit to the next generation of Canadians upon whom all of us rely. The evidence in this Bill and others is that the Government's purpose and intention is to strip the funding from higher education, from the co-operative programs which are federal and provincial, for one simple purpose-to create programs directly administered by Ottawa in contravention of the spirit of the Constitution which, it claims, will have long-term job benefits and the cheques for which can be handed out by Liberal back-benchers in an attempt to be re-elected. That is precisely the purpose and ambition of this Bill. I am astounded that Liberal Members opposite expect anyone to swallow this claptrap.

speechtext:
In speaking to Bill C-12, which puts the six and five limits on the contributions of the federal Government to post-secondary education, I would like to respond to some of the remarks which were made yesterday by the Hon. Member for Mississauge South (Mr. Blenkarn). I had hoped at that time that I might have an opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). Time ran out and I did not have that opportunity. Today I want to point out that I was, to say the least, bemused by the concern that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South showed about the sanctity of contract. He talked about the contract between the provincial and federal Governments as it pertained to fiscal arrangements. He was very eloquent in his defence of a principle that you do not interrupt contracts, that if you make a deal you stick with it. He went on at great length about how horrible the federal Government was for breaking a contract.
I just wish that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South and all of his Progressive Conservative colleagues had shown the same respect for contracts when the original six and five Bill was brought before the House. That Bill broke contracts with railroad workers and public servants. It broke contracts galore. We did not hear anything then about the sanctity of contract then from the Hon. Member for Mississauga South.
As far as the Progressive Conservatives are concerned, there are contracts and there are contracts. The same is true of the Liberal Government. This morning in committee we heard that one reason there is a three-year waiting period for doing anything about extra billing is that Ontario has a three-year
January 31, 1984

contract with the doctors. You must not touch a contract with doctors or with the provinces, but if you want to intervene in a contract to reduce benefits for workers, railroaders and public servants, that is different. They do not count when it comes to the reckoning of the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberals. I just wanted to put that offensive irony on the record.
I am against the Bill to apply six and five to post-secondary education. I have been against all the six and five Bills. I am against them on principle. My colleagues and I do not pick and choose according to what we think will be to our political advantage, like the Tories don't mind when contracts with workers are broken, but when it comes to pensioners and the provinces, it is a different story. We do not talk out of both sides of our mouths on this issue as do our colleagues to the right.
With regard to the six and five program, it is particularly irritating-and I have had constituents call me about this- that the Liberal Government has stuck six and five stickers on everything. People working for Canada Post receive a cheque with six and five in the corner. No matter where you go, you find a six and five sticker.
I realize that this is not a terribly substantive point, but the Government, realizing the amount of opposition that there was to this program, should not be so nervy. It should not stick six and five stickers all over the place, rubbing the noses of workers into the fact that it managed to pass the six and five program over the opposition of the NDP and with the co-operation of the Progressive Conservatives.
I wish to deal with some of the other matters in connection with Bill C-12. The separation of federal health care funding and post-secondary education is something I agree with. It was recommended by the all-Party task force on federal-provincial arrangements. It will make for easier accountability as to what the federal Government is providing for health care on the one hand and post-secondary education on the other. Being able to distinguish what goes to health care and what goes to postsecondary education is long overdue.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South that the two-thirds one-third is an arbitrary figure. It was arrived at by the federal Government during or after the 1977 negotiations. It is partly because it is an arbitrary figure that it is so difficult to determine on a province by province basis which provincial governments are living up to their previous commitments to post-secondary education, which provincial Governments use the federal Government contribution to permit their traditional amount of the burden with regard to post-secondary education decrease, and which provincial Goverments are increasing their commitment to post-secondary education.
I do not think there is any doubt that regardless of one's opinion about the wisdom and the rightness of the six and five program, in this case as it pertains to post-secondary education, there are provinces which have not passed on federal funding in the full amount to the post-secondary education sector. These provinces have allowed their contribution to this sector to atrophy as a result of federal contributions. But six and five funding for post-secondary education is not the
Established Programs Financing answer. As much as that happens to be a problem and as much as I sympathize with the federal Government in its desire for greater accountability and more visibility of federal spending on post-secondary education, the answer is not to put a six and five limit on federal funding. It does not increase accountability. It does not increase visibility. It does not benefit postsecondary education sector or federal-provincial relations. What does it do?
I can see some of the problems which the federal Government has with respect to post-secondary education. However, I do not think that six and five is the answer. It is indiscriminate. I already explained why I think it is difficult to make overall judgments about what the provinces are doing province by province in the post-secondary education sector. Six and five is a totally indiscriminate solution, if it is a solution at all, which it is not. It treats every province the same regardless of its commitment to post-secondary education, regardless of its needs, regardless of whether it is a have not or a more affluent province. On the basis that it is completely indiscriminate, this Bill deserves our opposition.
Any diminishing of commitment to post-secondary education on the part of any level of government comes at a particularly tough time for those who benefit from postsecondary education, that is mainly young people in the short-run but society as a whole in the long-run.
There is very high enrolment in our universities. The professional faculties cannot admit all of those who would like to attend. The arts and science faculties are busting at the seams. There are increases in tuition fees and incidental fees, that is, the many ways which universities get money out of students. They are really user fees for services which the universities provide. In addition, there are cutbacks at the federal level and at the provincial level in support of post-secondary education.
All of this is at a time when we have the highest youth unemployment in decades. Students are in double jeopardy. They cannot get into universities like they used to and even if they do get in, they can hardly afford to stay there. In the summer they cannot get a job. What are they supposed to do? Six and five in post-secondary education does not address that problem. Neither does all the hoopla around the Ministry of Youth. It is just a way of providing a public relations response to the problems of young people in this country rather than real solutions.
There is a trend in the country toward universities once again becoming a place that only people of means can afford to attend. Only the rich need apply, as the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky) said. That was a trend we conquered in many respects from the mid to late 1960s and into the 1970s. I know there were many people in Transcona, where I come from, who were the first of their families to go to university. They were able to do so sometimes because of the determination of parents who saved and made it possible. There was also an abundance of summer work in those days and good summer jobs were not that hard to come by. People could work in the summer and save. But there were also in the late 1960s and early 1970s, thanks to the provincial govern-

January 31, 1984
Established Programs Financing
ment in co-operation with the federal Government, more student loans available, more bursaries. We saw at that time, as I experienced it anyway, more and more people going to university who might not otherwise have been able to go. There was a kind of egalitarian bubble so far as enrolment at universities was concerned. I am not saying that that has disappeared altogether, but I am saying that we are going in the direction where that kind of equal access and opportunity, in which we took so much pride, is in danger. Action has to be taken, and applying six and five to post-secondary education is hardly a reasonable response to that situation.
This Bill also gives us an opportunity to reflect on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements as a whole, Mr. Speaker, which is what Bill C-12 is a part of. This Bill changes the title, and I think that is a good idea. I think it is much more useful to call it federal transfers for health care and post-secondary education than to call it federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. People might now have a ghost of a chance of knowing what we are talking about. I would like to see more language changes in this direction as far as Bills are concerned, indeed as far as laws are concerned, so that what we are talking about here can become more comprehensible to people in general.
The application of six and five to the federal contributions to post-secondary education we see another example of unilateral action on the part of the federal Government. In April, 1982, the federal Government reduced transfer payments to the provinces by the amount which had been put in there in 1977 as compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee. There was no renegotiation, just unilateral reduction and withdrawal of funds. This was on top of a unilateral imposition of a new equalization formula, which hurt the Province of Manitoba and Quebec in particular. There we have two unilateral actions, and then we had the application of six and five to post-secondary education. Really all the Government is doing now is legalizing what it did almost 18 months ago when it moved to the six and five program.
We have a history of unilateral actions, all of which have had the effect of taking money away from the provinces. We have the cutback in April, 1982, the imposition of a new equalization formula, and the application of six and five to post-secondary education. Therefore, the federal Government has a lot of explaining to do when it gets self-righteous with the provinces about what is going on in various sectors, whether health care or post-secondary education. This does not make right what the provinces do, it does not mean their response to federal cutbacks is always right. Indeed, it is more often than not wrong because they tend to use those cutbacks as a political cover for making decisions they would make in any case, but now they make them and blame the federal Government. This is particularly true in health care but also has ramifications in post-secondary education. On the one hand the federal Government has to be stern in requiring provinces to meet conditions like accountability and visibility. On the other hand, I think it has to demonstrate a willingness to re-open questions of funding and not act continually in this
unilateral fashion as far as health care and post-secondary education are concerned.
That is another thing I wanted to raise this afternoon, Mr. Speaker regarding this completely inadequate response to the crisis in post-secondary education. Educators across the country have been calling for a royal commission on post-secondary education. All the time I was on the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements educators came before us, such as the Canadian Association of University Teachers and the Association of Universities and Colleges, who all felt long before we got to this point that much more attention needed to be paid to the role of post-secondary education and to the various expectations being placed on the post-secondary education sector of this country. The Government did not respond to those requests. It has not initiated any major re-evaluation of post-secondary education. All we have seen is the limiting of federal funding. That hardly constitutes an adequate response, Mr. Speaker, and is one of the reasons why we will be opposing this Bill consistent with our opposition to all the six and five Bills this Government has brought in.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could the Hon. Member advise the House of his view concerning the revenue guarantee being removed from the transfer payments in 1982? At that time it was estimated to be about $500 million, but there has been indexing since then. Has the Hon. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, what applying six and five to post-secondary education transfers does is to make matters worse because it applies to a transfer which is already calculated on a diminished base thanks to the removal of the money attributable to the revenue guarantee in 1982. My view of that money at that time, and still today, is that it ought to have been regarded as money for health care and post-secondary education. In my view that is the position the parliamentary task force took. We pointed out, though, that there was an irony in that the federal Government, by deciding in 1982 not to regard that money as being for health care and post-secondary education, was in effect abandoning a position it had taken for five years. It had argued with the provinces that this was money for health care and post-secondary education. Then the provinces, which always said it was not for health care and post-secondary education, when the federal Government cut it back, said that it was for health care and post-secondary education. I guess this is the way it works, Mr. Speaker. Let me just say, oh what a tangled web we weave! Here we have the provincial Government arguing the federal position and the federal Government arguing the provincial position.
There is no question that the removal of the revenue guarantee has certainly been complicated by the six and five program which applies to a transfer which is already calculated on a diminished base. That is something that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and other Ministers
January 31, 1984

in this Government will never admit. After 1982 they kept talking about a 13 per cent increase. It was only a 13 per cent increase if you did not take into account the fact that the base had been diminished in the first place. If you took that into account, it turned out to be only a 4 per cent increase.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

Mr. Speaker, I cannot confirm the figures but there is no question that this is the direction in which the federal Government is going. On this issue at least I have a tendency to trust the calculations of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South. If he says the figure is $330 million, perhaps that is what it is. A couple of days ago the Hon. Member for Mississauga South made the argument that the money the provinces collect as a result of tax point transfers is not allocated money and that because they collect those taxes, the money is theirs. He forgets that the reason they are able to collect those moneys in the first place is that the federal Government transferred the points to them for a specific purpose.
In my view, anything which diminishes the cash transfer from the federal Government to the provinces increases the likelihood that such interpretations of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements as the one which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South tries to put forward might be believed. I think that would be unfortunate. I agree with the majority on the task force that all the money that is transferred to the provinces, whether it be in the form of cash or in the form of tax point transfers, has to be calculated in relation to what the federal Government is spending on health care and postsecondary education.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened to the remarks of many speakers in this debate, including the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell), the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. Lewycky), the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) and the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley). Each Member addressed the subject matter of the debate in a very relevant and important fashion. As I interpreted their remarks, none was picking quarrels with the provinces or with federal government standards. Instead they were trying to plead the case of the student, who at this time needs money as it has probably not been needed in the last 25 years in this country.
I rather bemoan the fact that the province which perhaps has the most to fear from this in its tax structure and budget balancing process at the moment is Manitoba where the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill has his constituency. I think he will regret taking the stand he has taken here inasmuch as he feels that all the evils are on his right and that he is not facing them. I think he should reconsider that stand because it is unwise.
I should like to put some figures on the record which will outline the position I want to take. I should like you to understand Mr. Speaker, that the changes are very significant in terms of dollars. If we look at the 1983-84 loss to the various provinces, we find that Newfoundland is losing $2.7 million; Prince Edward Island, $.6 million; Nova Scotia, $4.1 million; and New Brunswick, $3.3 million. If Bill C-12 is passed, in 1984-85 Newfoundland will lose $6.1 million; Prince Edward, $1.3 million; Nova Scotia, $10 million; and New
Brunswick, $4 million. This is happening at a time when the finances of those provinces are very seriously strained. They are having great difficulty in balancing their budgets or even approaching a responsible deficit at this moment in time. One finds, if one takes a look at some other statistics, that the programs under the established financing structure, without federal meddling, reached a point when they were bearing roughly 27 per cent of the total cost of provincial health and post-secondary education spending. However, from 1979-80 through to the 1982-83 Budget, that has dropped from 27 per cent to roughly 21.5 per cent. That is a very significant change in both the post-secondary education and in the cost of health care. The federal contributions to those services have declined from 1978-79 by over 5 per cent. If one looks at the percentage of health and PSE spending in another source, one comes up with exactly the same figure. I regret very much, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the areas which has been attacked as an opportunity for federal savings.
Again one finds that in 1979-80, by a federal estimate, the federal Government was assuming 31.3 per cent of the budgets of the provinces. It is now, in 1983-84, estimating it will assume 24.5 per cent of those same expenditures. That is down 7 per cent of the total expenditures of the province as the grants have been reduced, and it refers to Manitoba as well as it refers to the other provinces of Canada. This will give the provinces some rather serious difficulties in financing their requirements.
I checked some of the things that were said when I was in New Brunswick, and I first want to blow a hole in the idea that the announcement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) that we were going to receive an additional $769 million in 1983-84 was made in a very inaccurate way. These are the comments which have been made to me by a gentleman in New Brunswick who knows what he is talking about: the Throne Speech reference was made to an increase in federal funding for EPF. This was followed by a press release issued by the Minister of Finance which indicated that the provinces would receive an additional $769 million in 1983-84, New Brunswick's share being $21 million. I have discussed this matter with federal officials and have been able to confirm the following facts: one, this is not new federal money in the sense of a policy change as far as EPF is concerned. In other words, the federal Government is not in any way changing the EPF formula to result in increased payments to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education. The so-called "windfalls" are adjustments to the federal spending estimates. In other words, the $21 million referred to for New Brunswick is a re-estimate of the federal EPF spending in New Brunswick over and above the federal Budget estimate of last April. It is a measure of the inaccuracy of the federal Budget estimate for EPF made last April which we in fact knew was low at the time, and we had incorporated those adjustments in our budgeting process. It was not new money for the provinces in any way.
January 31, 1984

The so-called increase will do nothing, as far as the revenues of New Brunswick are concerned, that has not already been budgeted for. For some time now we have been anticipating an increase in EPF funding because of revised GNP figures. As a point of fact, the moneys referred to as a "windfall" for New Brunswick have been built into our current revenue forecast, and we are not in fact receiving largesse from the bounty of the federal Government in an additional way. 1 believe all of Canada assumed that the federal Government had given $769 million more than it ever had intended to, when in fact the formula which governed the grant dictated that that $769 million be made as an adjustment to federal estimates in its budget process. It is quite an error, $769 million.
Let me refer to what EPF is all about. And we are dabbling, meddling with EPF in this Bill. It was to provide long-term financing certainty to both levels of Government. It indexed federal contributions to the average growth of the national economy during the prior three years. The federal Budget of November 1981 proposed removing over $5 million from EPF over a five-year period to 1987. This was legislated within seven days of the expiry of the five-year guarantee. The unilateral decision of the federal Government to eliminate the revenue guaranteeing component of EPF reduced Ottawa's transfers by almost $1 billion in 1982-83 and an ever rising amount in subsequent years. This, of course, applies to postsecondary education.
The federal Government has recently announced its intention to split the EPF block fund into two components and to cap the growth of the per capita federal contributions for higher education at 6 per cent in 1983-84 and 5 per cent in
1984-85, with no indication of federal plans for the future. The implications of this are, first, that it leads to long-term financial uncertainty for the provinces; second, the split between health and post-secondary education is being done on the basis of the outdated and arbitrary 1975-76 ratio; and, third, by 1987, the provinces would lose $5,304 million through elimination of the revenue guarantee component and $911 million through the proposed cutting of money to post-secondary education, for a total of $6,215 million by 1987. Even if you come from Birds Hill that is not peanuts, Mr. Speaker. That is the situation.
I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that 1 was always one who favoured block funding, and it eventually became the policy of the Government of Canada, accepted amicably by the provinces of Canada, with the understanding that the federal Government was through meddling in those areas of responsibility which were provincial, such as post-secondary education, health care services and so on. It was through meddling. The formula had been written, it had been agreed to, and the provinces anticipated that it would be respected. However, in 1982, the provinces were advised very arbitrarily that in fact they could not expect to receive the same contributions which they had received and that there would be changes.
The consequence of this to New Brunswick has been very serious. We find that the provincial expenditures of the Province of New Brunswick have gone to $712 million since this
Established Programs Financing agreement was made. That is an increase, Mr. Speaker, of $294 million, as the services have been rendered by the Province of New Brunswick as best the federal Government could in accordance with its standards. That is the increase in the province's costs. The federal contribution, on the other hand, since 1979-80, has gone up by only $35 million. Therefore, the Province of New Brunswick is spending an additional $294 million for 1982-83, and the federal share of that has only gone up by $35 million. This certainly refuted all the good intentions of the Established Programs Financing policy which have been worked out in the block funding structure. In 1979-80 the share of the provincial expenditures as a total was 41.1 per cent. In 1982-83 it dropped to 29.1 per cent, a 12 per cent decline in total revenues for the provinces of Canada in that period of time. This is something which I submit to you the provinces cannot accept. The first major provincial shared cost program was hospital services. This program, introduced in 1958, provided for the federal Government to cover about one-half of the cost of approved hospital services, with the provinces covering the other half. In the late sixties the medicare program was introduced. Here again the federal Government agreed to cover, on average, half the cost of the provincial medicare program. According to the figures that I have already given you, they have not approached that figure in recent years.
The third major shared cost program involved federal grants for post-secondary education. In 1967 the federal Government offered to pay the provinces 50 per cent of the operating costs of post-secondary education institutions. The original agreements worked fairly well through the 1960s, but problems began to emerge in the 1970s. The provinces were having difficulty coping with the rigid program and spending guidelines laid down by the federal Government, which in many cases directed provincial spending to high cost rather than to less expensive program areas. The federal Government was concerned about the open-ended nature of its financial involvement in which it had to match provincial spending. Beginning in 1972 the federal Government began to take steps to reduce its financial commitments when it placed a cap on its contributions for post-secondary education. The introduction of caps and ceilings was totally contrary to the contract and spirit of the block funding structure which had been adopted. It was not within the intent of either the federal Government or the provinces that caps should be imposed, but rather that the indices of Canada would outline and define the responsibilities of the federal Govermment.
The 1977 arrangements replaced federal conditional grants to the provinces in support of medicare, hospital services and post-secondary education with a new program, namely the EPF. That has not worked either. With EPF, federal contributions were no longer determined by provincial program expenditures as they were before, but were tied to the rate of growth in Canada's economy. This gave the federal Government greater certainty about its financial commitments. Of equal importance, it placed an upper limit on its financial obliga-

January 31, 1984
Established Programs Financing
tions. This less attractive financial arrangement was made acceptable to the province because the federal Government assured them that EPF would give provincial Governments more flexibility in program decisions. Having put themselves in this position, Mr. Speaker, the provinces were asked to seek ways to make more effective use of the provinces money as it related to health care and post-secondary education. This meant the provinces were free to manage their health care and post-secondary education programs in their own way.
For the most part the provinces favoured the move although it was recognized that there would be some small reduction in the total moneys paid by the federal Government to the provinces. One of the key features of the arrangements was that it was designed to produce long-term certainty-please note that-for both the federal and provincial Governments. The federal Government obtained certainty that no matter how much the province spent on these programs its contributions would not exceed the growth of the national economy. The provinces obtained certainty that the federal Government would refrain from applying arbitrary caps and limits to its contribution and therefore could plan accordingly.
EPF worked fairly well over the five year period from 1977 to 1982. However, over that period, and within the lasts year, the federal Government has done much to destroy the principles on which EPF was based. It has launched a counter-productive quarrel with the provinces and caused serious distrust between the provinces and the national Government. Less than two years after it convinced the provinces to accept the EPF agreement, the federal Government wanted to change its terms and thereby reduce the EPF payments to the provinces. On this occasion the provinces successfully resisted cuts to EPF, but the federal Government responded by cutting other transfer payments and terminating discussions for new block funding arrangements for social services. Mr. Speaker, this does not look to me like a Government that wants to get along with the people, the voters and the governments of Canada.
In the 1981 federal Budget the Government of Canada announced its plan to cut over $5 billion from EPF funding over the period of 1982 to 1987. This cut was implemented in the spring of 1982 contrary to the recommendations of all the provinces, the Economic Council of Canada and an all-Party parliamentary task force chaired by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) in New Brunswick. Contrary to all of these recommendations the cut was implemented. The federal Minister of Finance announced that federal EPF contributions would be arbitrarily capped in so far as post-secondary education was concerned in 1983. We have that cap at a point in time when young people who cannot find jobs are seeking to improve their standards of earning opportunity by attending post-secondary institutions. Mr. Speaker, the time when potential students most need the money which would have ordinarily flowed from this program is a strange time indeed to put a cap on education. I bemoan the fact that this has happened at this particular point in time.
There have been some increments in those payments, but the fact of the matter is that although federal payments have been
increasing, they are not keeping pace with New Brunswick's spending needs, particularly in the health care field, which have been increasing, according to demands of the federal Government, federal standards and the Minister of Health of Canada (Miss Begin), at a rate which far outpaces the inflationary rate of this country today. The result is that the federal contributions as a percentage of provincial spending are falling, and if present trends continue, will fall for some time to come. As an example, the federal support of provincial spending on health care and post-secondary education peaked at 41 per cent and fell to less than 30 per cent by 1982-83.
I would like to give those who do not care about the provinces and the provincial taxpayers a little bit of information on what the tax rates are in the Atlantic provinces. Mr. Speaker, you are going to wonder why the Minister for New Brunswick, the former Premier of Nova Scotia and the former Leader of the Liberal Party in Prince Edward Island, sat idly by on your right while these things happened to the tax structure of Atlantic Canada. The gasoline tax is 9.8 cents per litre in Newfoundland and P.E.I. In Nova Scotia it is 8.8 and in New Brunswick 8.1. Excepting only Quebec, these are the highest taxes on gasoline of any part of Canada. In Newfoundland the sales tax is a burdensome 12 per cent. In New Brunswick, P.E.I. and Nova Scotia it is 10 per cent. The next highest is Quebec with a 9 per cent sales tax. These are the burdens which our provincial taxpayers are carrying. Mr. Speaker, might I have unanimous consent to continue for a couple more minutes please?

In Newfoundland the income tax rate is 60 per cent of the federal tax, in P.E.I., 52.5 per cent, in Nova Scotia, 56.5 per cent; and in New Brunswick, 58 per cent. These are, without any doubt, the highest provincial income tax rates in Canada. The cutbacks in these grants for the established programs Financing are going to transfer additional payments on provinces which are already the highest taxed provinces in Canada. They are transfering these costs to those provinces at the rate of tens of millions of dollars which they do not have. Mr. Speaker, does the Government have any concern whatsoever for the financial future of those provinces with that tax burden as it changes this financing program as it relates to both health and post-secondary education?
I submit to you that as the various Ministers have been badgering the provinces, including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) and the Minister of Finance when he falsely announced his $769 million, this is transparent deceit in trying to transfer the burden of performance to the
January 31, 1984

provinces and accusing them of everything but good government while depriving them of the historic means which has provided them with the financial capability to serve.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Fraser Valley West) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX ACT EXEMPTION FOR SMALL FARM HOLDINGS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the retention of productive and potentially productive small holdings in agricultural production is of value and, that the government should consider the advisability of repealing Section 31 of the Income Tax Act which threatens the retention of such productivity, lifestyle and land use.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the issue of small farm holdings, production on them and the issue of taxation of that production is what my motion refers to today. There is a smaller issue which has been in focus in the House and throughout the country that relates to aggressive, repressive tax assessors acting with unconscionable and unfair pressure, brought on to excesses by a bankrupt government with a big stick and a desperate need to fill an empty coffer as a result of its own wastes and its own excesses. In fact, as a result of the kind of application of the Income Tax Act in this and many other cases, the Government is cutting off its nose to spite its face. These small farm holdings have a capacity to produce food and provide a lifestyle. The land on these small farm holdings is becoming unproductive because the incentive to make them produce is being withdrawn.
The smaller issue is the tax issue itself. I do not pretend that the motion which I bring forward will in fact answer or solve the problem in itself. This particular motion brings the subject matter forward which will have to be discussed. It may not only be Section 31 but several different parts of the income Tax Act which will have to be amended in order to get back to the basic principle that was intended by this particular tax incentive, or disincentive as it has become.
Hopefully, by bringing this motion forward today we will bring the matter to the attention of the Government once again. 1 want to commend highly my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway), and other colleagues from across the country who have been pursuing this matter persistently in the House with respect to the problem of producing on small farm holdings and the tax which in fact destroys that production. It is a difficult equation and the answer is not easy. It is not easy to find a balance between production, taxation and land use that is fair. We
Income Tax Act
know now that it is not working today. The small farmers and businessmen who are trying to struggle to create agricultural products and this lifestyle from a little extra production are experiencing in fact just symptoms of something that is gravely wrong with a system that is in need of a major overhaul, redefiniton and readjustment.
It does come back to a question of land use. It would seem that in this, the second largest country in the world with one of the lowest density populations in the world, the taxation on production and on land would not have a negative effect on production since we have so much of that land. It is a resource which we must protect as an element of production in our society. The federal Government does that through an incentive in the Income Tax Act to keep the land productive. It may well be that we will have to get rid of this Government to begin the correction and to allow this lifestyle and land use to continue. There is in
Canada a sense of fairness, and those who produce know that we have a system of taxation, a Robin Hood system. If you produce, fine. Not only do you produce, but you pay a tax and maybe you pay too much tax. But taxpayers will keep paying that tax as long as it seems to be fair. That inherent line of fairness in the Fraser Valley in British Columbia at least, and across the country as I hear from my colleagues, has that narrow line. It has not been stepped across. It has been strided across and it has been broken. That is causing symptoms, namely the anger of the small farmer and the small land holder who has worked and struggled to maintain his production and who sees his capacity destroyed. He says, "It is not worth it. I cannot be bothered. I will not produce these few extra head of cattle. I will not produce this extra produce. It is not worth it". This Bill is of great concern in my riding of Fraser Valley West. As I have said, the nature of my riding is that of a suburban area. It is one of the fastest growing communities in British Columbia, in fact, in Canada. I see the pressure every day. The oceans and mountains which give Vancouver its unique beauty also forces expansion of the community from the ocean up the valley into the lush Fraser Valley. Every day more houses are being built on prime farmland. Every day more acres of valuable agricultural land are taken out of food production and out of that lifestyle. Ultimately, the society I want to create for Canada and I think the people I represent want to create is the kind of society that gives a lifestyle of maximum opportunity. This lifestyle is high density for many, low density for many and a lifestyle which ensures that if you just want to live in an apartment or a condominium, you have that choice. But what if you want to live on a small farm and maybe do another job at the same time as you add a little production, in fact, do a second job while others in the community go to movies, to various shows, nightclubs and so forth? What if you, on the other hand, milk a few cows and raise a few beef, put a little extra feed in seven days a week, produce a little bit and earn a little bit extra in side income, why should there not be some incentive to earn extra income from that second job? Why is there not a category for a person working at one job while at the same time he tries to build some side income from farming? Perhaps he might want to make farming into a full time occupation.
There was some hope for the individual in our society that he could still do that. But that has been taken away. To go into a big farm process is almost out of the question for most Canadians now. There is an opportunity for small farm holders and for some part time farmers. I want to make sure the Income Tax Act takes that into account and provides definition and incentive for them. If it does not happen, this unchecked growth will see the lower mainland become a megalopolis from Vancouver to Chilliwack. It will be like Los Angeles. Los Angeles might be an interesting city but it is an absolute tragedy from a planter's point of view as it has spread its pavement, freeways and houses for miles and miles up the

valley. What happened as housing spread out and as pollution grew? One can see pollution hanging over the city. I do not want Vancouver, Toronto or Ottawa to be like that. It is hard for a civil servant, a Deputy Minister and others to interpret that because in Ottawa the National Capital Commission preserves open spaces and preserves a particular lifestyle. It lets us feel comfortable and lets our city breathe. I want to see the city in which I live be allowed to breathe as well. Part of that process is right here.
We can avoid the problem of urban sprawl with careful planning. Small agricultural holdings also provide an alternative lifestyle that we seek. This means we will have to allow these small farmers to have a full write-off. It is a business principle. When is an expense of a production an expense of production? If I am raising high quality race horses or if I am raising high quality cattle or breeding stock I might invest thousands and thousands of dollars. I have one constituent who hires 10 or 15 people. He would hire another five or ten. But why do it? He cannot write the expense off as an income tax deduction because he is classified as a hobby farmer. He has only ten acres. But he has a million-dollar business going. That, however, cannot be claimed as an expense. He cannot claim against his other income. It is, indeed unfortunate.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and express the concerns of individual after individual. I could speak of the associations that have expressed concern. I will present petitions in the House of Commons from the small farm agricultural holding throughout my riding. Who will hear them? Who will receive them? Is our democracy dead here that these people cannot be heard, that there cannot be action carried forward? subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX ACT EXEMPTION FOR SMALL FARM HOLDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the principles enunciated in this Private Member's Bill. It is an issue about which I feel very strongly.
I would like to look at the impact of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act. It is a provision designed to limit the losses which persons can claim against other income when those losses result from farming operations. There are very few other provisions in the Income Tax Act which restrict losses in a business from being deducted against other types of income. In essence, it is a unique provision aimed particularly against certain types of farmers.
What was the purpose of the provision? When it was included in 1952, it was assumed that we would prevent
Income Tax Act
so-called rich people or people with a lot of money from investing in farms and writing off their losses against executive incomes of, say $200,000 a year-the so-called hobby farmers. In effect, this is saying that farming is not a legitimate business. If those rich people had purchased hardware stores, invested in the textile industry, started a shoe shop, a grocery store or whatever and lost money, they would have been able to deduct their losses. We are putting farmers into a very unique category.
Who are the farmers right now who are facing economic problems and are suffering in the country? To a large measure they are red meat farmers on smaller marginal holdings, smaller lands which are not amenable to rich cash crop operations. What happens? Either the farmers go out of business or they show some initiative by obtaining jobs as well as carrying on farming operations. They take jobs in town and supplement their farm incomes. The impact of Section 31 is to discourage that type of hard work and initiative, because the moment farmers are earning more income from other jobs to make the farms pay, from working in town eight hours a day, 40 hours a week and then spending another 40 hours working on the farm, they lose their farming losses and are restricted under the provisions of Section 31.
Are we attempting to encourage initiative and hard work, or are we more concerned about what was once a perceived loophole? I would like to refer to a Saskatchewan couple of whom I am aware. The wife is an assistant veterinarian and the husband works in an electronics plant. They want to invest in a small-acreage horse farm. They want to raise horses and sell them as yearlings. If they cannot deduct their losses because they already have other jobs, they will be unable to become involved in the business. We are not only hurting people who are in farming and take jobs to supplement their incomes during these tough times for farmers, we are stopping additional people who have an interest in farming from becoming involved.
As far as rich persons are concerned, we are not concerned about persons making $100,000 a year and wanting to become involved in farming as a hobby. We already have built-in safeguards in the system to protect such individuals. Under the present law they cannot operate farms without an expectation of profits and still deduct losses, nor can one in any other business. One has to have a reasonable expectation of profits. That is the safeguard.
A further safeguard, if we wanted to include one, would be the "safe haven" type of rules such as they have in the United States where one has to earn a profit so many years out of so many years. If we wanted a little more certainty in our tax laws, that would be the way to explore plugging up any loophole or curing any problems which might arise.
Let us look at the impact of such farmers becoming involved in smaller acreage marginal lands which support horses or beef but not heavy cash crops. What will be the impact on employment? These types of operations require labour. They are labour-intensive. They need people to build fences, to do the feeding, to do the mucking, to do the sowing, to look after

January 31, 1984
Income Tax Act
cattle when they are giving birth, to look after the young horses and to do the selling. Who are the types of people they employ? By and large the people employed on these types of farms are unskilled labour but people who have a commitment to the outdoors, to animals and to the land. These are the people who need jobs in this time when technology is taking over and they almost require Ph.D.s to obtain jobs in certain areas.
Who will benefit if we were to adopt the principles mentioned in the Bill and to reform what I think is an antiquated provision in Section 31 of the Income Tax Act? In summary, farmers facing problems today who want to supplement their incomes by working in town or elsewhere would benefit. These are the type of people who need our help. Second, we would bring into better use much of the marginal farmland which we find in Ontario and in other parts of Canada. Third, we would be increasing employment as these are labour-intensive operations. Fourth, by abolishing this one restriction in the Income Tax Act, we would be generating on the whole more tax revenue. More money would be going into these marginal farms instead of going into condominiums in Florida. More people would be buying small farms, which creates expenditures in rural communities at the feed or supply store. More people would be hired who would be paying more income tax. Fewer tax assessors would be running around worrying about these types of accounts.
Let us recognize that farming is a business like any other business but, more than that, it is also a way of life which we should want to encourage and preserve. We should stop penalizing farmers who have to take jobs to keep their farms going. This is one instance when all farm groups are united and unanimous in their recommendations for changes to Section 31.
In conclusion, we should either abolish Section 31 outright or, failing that, a reasonable alternative is one that was presented by many farming groups, that is, to increase the restricted farm loss from $5,000 per year to an amount which reflects the realities of today. That $5,000 per year amount was put into effect in 1952 and has remained unchanged. Surely it is time, if we do not abolish it, that we at least bring it up to inflationary standards.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX ACT EXEMPTION FOR SMALL FARM HOLDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to rise in support of the Private Member's motion before us which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the retention of productive and potentially productive small holdings in agricultural production is of value and, that the Government should consider the advisability of repealing Section 31 of the Income Tax Act which threatens the retention of such productivity, lifestyle and land use.
The section has come up for a great deal of criticism and discussion. The recent court case of Paul Graham of Lanark County gives us some hope that the section will be opened up for interpretation. The judgment was given by Mr. Justice Cattanach. His judgment was very fair and objective with regard to how he viewed Section 31. He reviewed the various steps of the case before it got to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Mr. Justice Cattanach said that the previous court said that the section is meaningless and incomprehensible and therefore should not be applied to the detriment of the taxpayer. Mr. Justice Dickson, who made the first ruling which had been appealed by the Department of National Revenue, did not accede to that submission for to do so would be in effect to write the section out of the statute. Accordingly, he made the valiant effort to make sense out of language where no sense existed, such as: "According to the ruling Section 13, which is now Section 31, but the material language thereof is unchanged." In construing the section, he said what the three clauses were. I would like to read them into the record so that people can make sense out of them. This is the section the Department is interpreting. I quote:
(1)	a taxpayer, for whom farming may reasonably be expected to provide the bulk of income or the centre of work routine. Such a taxpayer, who looks to farming for his livelihood, is free of the limitation of s. 13(1) in those years in which he sustains a farming loss.
(2)	the taxpayer who does not look to farming, or to farming and some subordinate source of income, for his livelihood but carries on farming as a sideline business. Such a taxpayer is entitled to the deductions spelled out in s. 13(1) in respect of farming losses.
(3)	the taxpayer who does not look to farming, or to farming and some subordinate source of income, for his livelihood and who carries on some farming activities as a hobby. The losses sustained by such a taxpayer on his non-business farming are not deductible in any amount.
Putting it into a little plainer English, it means that parttime farmers are generally restricted in the application of their farm losses subject to the interpretation by the Department and its auditor. The part-time farmer's loss is calculated as the lesser of the actual loss and $2,500 plus half of the loss in excess of $2,500 to a maximum of $5,000 in any one taxation year. Any remaining portion of the loss may only be applied against farm profits in the carry over period. Hobby farmers are not permitted to claim losses since they are not considered to be operating a business.
Because the question of the hobby farmer comes up often in the debate on Section 31, in my opinion hobby farmers should be treated the way they have been under that section. The Department's problem is deciding when a hobby farmer is no longer a hobby farmer. Those who have been running into difficulty with the Department are those like Paul Graham of Lanark County. He had a job, and I presume he continues to have a job, which employs him for 36 or 37 hours a week. He spends 40, 50 or 60 hours a week working the farm that he has built up. He has added to it over the years and is now generating gross income somewhere in the $60,000 to $80,000 range. He earns less than $30,000 at his other job.
January 31, 1984

It was fairly easy and clear-cut for the judge to make the decision he did, that Paul Graham was attempting to become a full-time farmer. He had the volume of business and at the moment of the assessment he was showing a loss. There was a downturn in the meat market. Hogs, his main enterprise, did not bring in enough money to cover his cost of production. There are other cases. I will read only one to show that Paul Graham was not an isolated case. This individual, who lives in Manitoba, said in part in his letter to Revenue Canada, and I quote:
I work a 37 Vi hour work week for Manitoba Hydro and approximately 40 to 50 hours a week on the farm. I travel home after hours and still manage to put in anywhere from six to eight hours on the farm during seeding, summer fallow and harvest time. I spend my four-week holiday plus about 30 to 40 hours on weekends Saturday and Sundays plus statutory holidays.
Since I took full operation of my dad's farm I replaced all the old machinery, cleared off most of the stones, cleared and opened up more land, thus increasing the value of the farm. I installed sewage and water, completely renovated my house and put up a workshop.
I was born and raised on the farm and because farm expenses have outstripped the farm income, as is well known, I set out to seek employment to supplement my family income.
1 am an hourly employee and could be laid off at any time. As I write this letter, 1 am presently laid off for a short period.
I feel the money I spend on upgrading and maintaining my farm is money spent on the local economy and is regenerated through the system for the good of the small businesses that are engaged in the farm machinery and supply sector.
1 don't accept the fact that you have judged my farm operation as a business that has no hope of ever becoming a profitable one. 1 feel since my small operation is financed by my hard work and determination of keeping it in the family and is not dependent on government grants, forgiveable loans, government bail-out, et cetera, 1 also feel that your decision is forbidding me to be an equal of having the right to deduct my expense from my income regardless of whether I make a profit or not.
And I also feel that 1 am not a sinner by not making a profit and if 1 am a sinner then I should be given the same recognition as many other sinners, just to name a few, Government of Canada, CNR, Air Canada and the list could go on.
That probably outlines the argument made by farmers who are attempting to operate small farms and make them into a manageable size in order that they can give up their job or look forward to the day when their off-farm job will no longer be available.
There is the problem of hobby farmers. As the motion suggests, it is time to reconsider the advisability of Section 31. We should open up the whole process and look at what we are doing to farmers, both the beginning category and the so-called viable category and some of our accelerated depreciation schedules which allow machinery to be written off the books much faster than it wears out. We should review our tax policy as it applies to investment tax credits which are an accelerated accelerated depreciation. As well, we should look at the whole policy of capital gains as it applies to agriculture. These items have been discussed many times in the House.
We look forward to the February 15 Budget which we hope will deal with some of these issues. In the unlikely event of that Budget speech tackling head-on these tax problems that affect farmers, we should pursue the motion before us today presented by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). We should refer its contents to the appropriate committee for discussion not only of Section 31, but of the
Income Tax Act
whole question of hobby farming, investment tax credits, capital gains and accelerated depreciation.
There are many farm groups with reservations about allowing too much of an increase in the amount of write-offs which a hobby farmer can have. They are somewhat fearful of large investors who come into agriculture looking for the fun of being farmers with a rural setting to go to on weekends combined with the advantage of writing off some of the profits of their other profession or business. In short, it makes for a very uneven competition in rural areas where legitimate farmers are attempting to make a living from the soil and contribute to their communities. They do not look kindly upon hobby farmers who come in from the city on weekends to do this, and we in this corner of the House do not think that increasing write-offs for genuine hobby farmers does anything for the rural community or for the investment potential of the whole country. We would restrict them to the part-time farmer and the farmer who is attempting to work his way into agriculture. The clear-cut hobby farmer who is out there because he decided to walk around the farm instead of walking around the golf course, well, we are not particularly anxious to see that in the part of the country I come from.

The trouble we are presently having is not so much the fault of the legislation as it is the attitude of the Department of

January 31, 1984
Income Tax Act
Revenue officials. A good example was typified by the National Film Board movie we saw on the Journal last night which certainly makes Orwell's prophesies virtually come true. The aggressiveness of the Department is not only seen in the farming community, it is seen right through the system. We on this side have brought up example after example over the last few weeks. In other words, he did not allow the auditors to go back and reassess any more than one year. If the present Minister would do this, we would not have this tremendous retroactive slap that people are getting at the present time. If you reassess for a four-year period it is absolutely impossible for some people to pay the resulting bill. I think the highest reassessment that I have seen was pretty close to $100,000, and most of them are $10,000 to $20,000.
Interestingly enough, Mr. Speaker, because I have done a fair bit of work concerning this section of the Income Tax Act, I get phone calls from people about tax problems. One of the most interesting I have had so far was over the last weekend. The person who contacted me had been a supervisor in one of the large regional offices of the Department. He told me that in British Columbia the quota system always was and still is in use. The only thing is that they have changed the name now to "Standards of Production". He gave me a good example of the pressures the quota system puts on auditors. When it looks as if an auditor is going to be short on his quota, he has a file of defunct or bankrupt companies he can dip into. He will pick a company that has been out of business for three or four years and do an audit. In the case this gentleman told me about it had been a company that had been out of business for three years. There was absolutely no chance that the Department would get any revenue from this account. They did the audit, the auditor reassessed the company for $90,000. This he added to his quota and pushed it on to the collection department. They in turn fiddled with it for a few days before finding out that the company was out of business. Then they used it for their quota. What I am saying is that the quota system still exists and there are all kinds of ways the system is being abused.
Section 31 is causing a good deal of grief in the agricultural community, Mr. Speaker. It has caused an awful lot of problems in my riding as well as in the riding of Fraser Valley West. I hope that in this upcoming Budget we will see a good positive change that will once and for all address this problem.
At this point I would like to move that the House refer the subject matter of this motion to the Standing Committee on Agriculture for further study.
