speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) for his approach to this subject in that he has a Private Member's Bill of his own in the works on this very topic. I believe that should be looked at in great detail.
I think I should correct the statement made by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) who indicated that Paul Graham comes from Lanark County. Actually he comes from Lambton County in my constituency. He is a constituent of mine so I have followed this case with him through the courts and I know what has been happening. He had been farming with his father when he was 19 years old, intending to become the operator of the farm. That was in 1962, when times were tough-there is the old saying that Tory times are tough times. Anyway, they lost the farm and Paul moved to the city where he went to work for Ontario Hydro. In 1963 he bought the farm in Lambton County. In time, he became an engineer for Ontario Hydro and put his money back into the farming operation. It was a very successful operation until last spring when the land was expropriated by the Ontario Government for the new Darcy McKeogh flood plain dam. Paul had to start again.
In order to put this in perspective, however, we must look at what has been happening in the farming sector. In about 1977, in the Province of Ontario 27 per cent of farmers had off-farm income. Today the figure is 45.8 per cent. The average income from off-farm jobs is $15,263 per year, but the average net income for all farmers from farms in Ontario is $2,095 per year. This shows that there is an urgent need for a system whereby farmers can supplement their incomes in the years when they are starting out.
I believe that there are other areas that should be examined as well, Mr. Speaker. We should consider the establishment of a registered savings plan whereby farmers could set money aside, tax free, to be applied as a downpayment on a farm or a small business. I have the same fears as the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin regarding hobby farmers taking over land and writing it off as an expense and simply having tenants on the farms. Consequently, I heartily endorse the suggestion by the Hon. Member for Willowdale and the proposal supported by many people in the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, that the limit be raised to reflect the inflationary spiral since 1950. There should be a counterbalance to ensure that the small farmer who wants to devote a lifetime to developing a farm has every opportunity to do so. The Act was put in place, however, because of the fears of farm organizations that very wealthy people would buy up the land in order to use it as a write-off for tax purposes.
I should like to support very strongly the proposal made by the Hon. Member for Willowdale that, rather than abolish that section of the Act, we update it to reflect the current values the inflation of the last 30 years has brought about. I hope that when the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin brings his Bill in, it will be drafted in such a way that we can support it and have it referred to a committee.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF TWO-INCOME FAMILIES. (B) TREATMENT OF SPOUSES OF DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES. (C) INFORMATION PROVIDED TO DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES
NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF TWO-INCOME FAMILIES. (B) TREATMENT OF SPOUSES OF DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES. (C) INFORMATION PROVIDED TO DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 19, Hansard records, at page 313, that I rose in my place to ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) a question about the reassessment of members of the families of employees of his Department. I would like at this stage to correct Hansard on my second question. It should read, "It is the spouse of the departmental employee ...", not as the record shows," . .. the spouse of the non-departmental employee . .." It was the spouse of a departmental employee who was at issue at that particular time.
The immediate issue, one of a series of issues which were being put to the Minister at that time, and which are still very much in the forefront, related to the way he was running his Department. I asked whether the Minister was aware, first of all, that assessments, checks or reviews were being carried out on the tax returns submitted by members of his employees' families, and if he was aware of this, why were such checks being carried out? The Minister indicated he was not aware that the families of his employees were being reassessed.
The second issue on that occasion, and it was raised separately, centered on the unusual, indeed, quite unacceptable practice and procedure which is presumably in force in the Victoria office, in any event, of informing the employee that his or her spouse's tax return is being examined or reassessed. As a preliminary question why should the rule of confidentiality, I must ask myself, be breached in the case of departmental employees when it is respected, or ought to be respected, with respect to all other citizens?
However, let me go back to the first issue, the class of persons whose tax returns are being re-examined such as members of the families of employees of the tax collection offices. It may be even broader than that, but why that particular class? I asked the supervisor, a regional director, who had come to call on me about this particular question, even before I took it up with the Minister. He said he considered it important that employees' records of tax collections should be "squeaky clean" on the grounds that the departmental officers can hardly go around pointing to others

January 31, 1984
Adjournment Debate
who are delinquent or actual offenders of the law unless those officials are themsleves wholly blameless before the law. That is one explanation, and I accept it. However, I do not accept the explanation in this particular case because it is not the employee of the Department who is being examined, Mr. Speaker, it is the spouse of an employee of the Department. They are two distinct individuals, or ought to be. I was seeking an answer as to whether there was a class of people who were being examined. Employees are one thing. The spouses of employees are quite another.
There is perhaps a more sinister explanation than the one given to me about the "squeaky cleanness" of the Department. That is, that the Department may not trust its employees and fears they may be passing on to their spouses some tax dodges, if you like, of one kind or another about which only a well qualified tax collector would be aware-not illegal dodges, but avoidances rather than evasions about which you and I, Mr. Speaker, might not be aware. Is that what the assessors were after? Is that why the spouses of the employees were being reassessed or re-examined? Were these signs of "extra smarts" that the taxpayer being reassessed might have displayed about which someone, without a tax collector as a spouse, would have been unaware? Is that what was behind the decision to single out the spouses of employees as a class ripe for reassessment and review?
I would like to come back to the issue of the breach of confidentiality. That is an important one. That aspect of the case is beyond dispute because the spouse who was being re-examined told me that the other spouse, who was the employee, had imparted this information in the course of a family conversation. I thought it was one of the absolutely unassailable guarantees that what is contained in a tax form is a matter between the tax department and the person who files the return. I think this guarantee rests on a statutory authority and that therefore, in this case, the Department could be accused, possibly even before a court, of breaking a trust guaranteed by law.
What if there had been some slight uncertainty as to the future of the marriage in this particular case? If the employee spouse was told that the non-employee spouse was being investigated could this not have been construed as an aggravation, a further threat to the marriage? Can a government Department condone such unwarranted interference in family affairs? If one spouse decides to tell the other, that is another matter. To parody something that was said in this House sometime before I came into it; the income tax Department has no place in the bedrooms of the nation. The offended party should have a chance to obtain redress for any damage that may have occurred by this unjustified intrusion into the affairs of the families of the employee.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there were two issues involved. The first is the decision about examining the affairs of the families of employees. That may be a legitimate one. The other issue is the breach of confidentiality. 1 think Mr. Speaker, that that
was absolutely inexcusable, and I feel that the Minister owes an apology to this particular person.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-TAX REASSESSMENT OF TWO-INCOME FAMILIES. (B) TREATMENT OF SPOUSES OF DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES. (C) INFORMATION PROVIDED TO DEPARTMENTAL EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tax Department naturally expects a very high standard of compliance from its own employees on the principle that anyone who has a responsibility for the enforcement of a law should be most scrupulous in the personal observation of that law. In some cases-and here we are talking about taxpayers in general, not just employees of the Department-the return of a taxpayer's spouse has to be taken into account when assessing the taxpayer's return itself.
The simplest example occurs when a child tax credit is claimed since the combined incomes of the claimant and the spouse determine the amount of any child tax credit. Or, as another example, certain provincial tax credits are payable only to the higher income earner in a marriage. A more complex example would arise where the taxpayer and the spouse are involved in a business partnership.
The Hon. Member has expressed concern about a possible violation of the confidentiality provision of the Act when a taxpayer has to be told something about the tax affairs of the spouse, or vice-versa. The Act contemplates certain kinds of circumstances when common sense dictates there has to be some such communication if the taxpayers involved are not to be left in the dark about the tax assessments that directly affect them.
I would like to quote the relevant words from paragraph 241 (4)(c) which allows the communication of information obtained under the Act concerning the income of a spouse:
-that is necessary for the purposes of determining any tax, interest, penalty or other amount payable by the taxpayer or any refund to which he is entitled.
I hope this information will set at rest any concerns about the violation of confidentiality restrictions that the Hon. Member may have felt.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-INCOME TAX ACT PROVISIONS- MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) DELAYS IN ADJUDICATING TAX ASSESSMENT APPEALS
NATIONAL REVENUE-INCOME TAX ACT PROVISIONS- MINISTER'S POSITION. (B) DELAYS IN ADJUDICATING TAX ASSESSMENT APPEALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had occasion on Friday, January 27 to ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) a question which had its foundation in my desire to expedite the process wherein objections filed by taxpayers as a consequence of assessments that had been issued against them might be dealt with in a fashion somewhat speedier than presently exists. The Minister's response to me at that time was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was in the House and had heard my remarks and accordingly would be governed by them.
It is important, with respect to this issue, that we understand the proceedings that are followed under the current provisions of the Income Tax Act wherein an assessment may be issued by the Minister for a variety of reasons, either as a conse-
January 31, 1984

quence of the supplying of information by the taxpayer to the Minister or otherwise. Upon the issuing of that assessment a collection process begins which the Minister has said in the House repeatedly has been somewhat expedited as a consequence of the fact that there are some $3.5 billion outstanding and unpaid to the Receiver General of Canada.
Of course, my question is how much of that is legitimately due and payable, not how much of that is owing legally, because I accept the Minister's figure. In determining how much is legitimately and legally ultimately due and owing it is important to have some regard to the current provisions of the Act as it relates to the issuing of assessments. In connection with this matter I would refer to the provisions of subsection 152(7) and 152(8) of the Income Tax Act. They provide as follows:
(7)	The Minister is not bound by a return or information supplied by or on behalf of a taxpayer and, in making an assessment may, notwithstanding a return or information so supplied or if no return has been filed, assess the tax payable under this Part.
Subsection 8 provides very significantly:
(8)	An assessment shall, subject to being varied or vacated on an objection or appeal under this Part and subject to a reassessment, be deemed to be valid and binding notwithstanding any error, defect or omission therein or in any proceeding under this Act relating thereto.
The very Act contemplates that assessments may have built therein errors or omissions which could easily give rise very clearly to tax being due and payable in law, whereas in fact and in substance ultimately, as decided by the objection proceedings or proceedings before the courts, they may be determined to be incorrect.
Accordingly, my submission to the Minister was to expedite the process at least at the objection stage so that the taxpayer might sooner learn how much of the tax that was originally owing as a consequence of the assessment should indeed be paid. As I have indicated, we know that once the assessment is issued and the collection process begins it takes a variety of forms, such as a garnishee which may be issued against the taxpayer, assets of the taxpayer which may be seized and sold, or a simple execution against the taxpayer may occur. This is all during the period when a valid objection may be outstanding.
The current process is that the taxpayer is entitled, within a period of 90 days from the date appearing on the Notice of Assessment, to issue and serve a notice of objection. That 90-day period clearly is within the control of the taxpayer in the event he wishes to expedite the process. He need only issue and serve his Notice of Objection at as early a date as possible. However, the objection process thereafter is out of his control.
The astounding thing is that the Minister of National Revenue has a full 180 days within which-internally within the Department of National Revenue-to consider the objection which has been filed. I point out that it is within that period of time that the collection process can begin and be concluded so that the assets of the taxpayers may indeed be stripped away from him. Accordingly, I urged the Minister to have some regard, simply from an administrative standpoint,
Adjournment Debate
to the plight of the taxpayer, and to see that his officials deal with the issues raised in the Notice of Objection at as early a date as possible.
Why are we concerned with these matters particularly today? It is, quite frankly, because this House has heard a variety, indeed a volume of cases dealing with actions by the Department of National Revenue arising as a consequence of quota systems that have been established, systems which are detrimental to the true collection of the ultimate amount of tax that should be paid by the taxpayers of Canada.
I resent the fact that the Minister stands in his place and tries to set one group of taxpayers against the other. He says there are some taxpayers who are obliged to pay their tax on a weekly, a biweekly or a monthly basis because they are employees and their tax is deducted at source, and there is another group of taxpayers who owe a total of $3.5 billion who are borrowing money from the Receiver-General or otherwise cheating their fellow taxpayers. This is simply not true. I question how much of the $3.5 billion ultimately will be due and payable.
On behalf of the taxpayers of Canada, I urge the Minister to speed up the process which would entitle those taxpayers so assessed to know at as early a date as possible what the true extent of their liability might be, hoping in that interim we will have an opportunity to defer the collection process which in many cases has become most offensive.
There have been systems established which could assist the Minister. One in particular was the Comscreen system developed by a gentleman by the name of Gerry Foxall of the Belleville district office of the Department, which would have seen a much more reasonable way of both evaluating the actions, from the standpoint of promotion, of assessors and at the same time zeroing in on those areas where tax might legitimately be collected. The Minister has failed to deal with that kind of a system and is using something that is antiquated and ineffective, a selection by lot and an allocation of files to a variety of assessors in fixing the quota with respect to the work they are to do. That, of course, is unsatisfactory.

The difficulties may arise because of unintended consequences. For example, an unintended loophole may be created or an unintended restriction

subtopic: FISHERIES-MANAGEMENT COSTS OF WEST COAST SALMON FISHERY. (B) NUMBER OF VESSELS ENGAGED IN COMMERCIAL SALMON FISHERY
FISHERIES-MANAGEMENT COSTS OF WEST COAST SALMON FISHERY. (B) NUMBER OF VESSELS ENGAGED IN COMMERCIAL SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, on January 24, I rose to confront the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) with the stark reality of an existence in the fishing industry on the West Coast that is intolerable. The value of a landed catch of salmon there is $240 million and it costs $84 million to run the Pacific Region Office, not including what it costs to run the Ottawa bureaucracy. That runs to a 35 per cent to 50 per cent cost for management. There is not another industry in the world that could tolerate that kind of industry management cost.
I pointed out to the Minister that when we had a free entry system of licensing in the industry we had about 20 new licences issued in a year. Once the Liberal Government instituted a buy-back program and restricted licences, that number ballooned to 45 licences a year. It boggles my mind to think that in a free entry system we could be getting 20 new licences but in a restricted entry the figure goes to 45.
I think there are serious questions we have to ask of the Minister about the conduct of his department. To my astonishment the Minister replied, and I shall quote from Hansard. He said:
The Hon. Member is right to say that already two buy-back programs have been implemented in the past and that has not prevented the participants in the fishery from over-investing and over-fishing to the point where today's stock has been the object of substantial pressure.
What he is saying is that it is not the Department's fault, it is not the Minister's fault, it is the fishermen's fault; they are to blame. This is the only manager in an industry that would ever blame the workers for being too productive. Almost every other industry would welcome that kind of productivity. However, this Minister blames the fishermen for being too productive, overlooking the fact that the officials of his Department are the ones who granted the licence which tolerated or brought about the over-fishing.
I want to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, some very stark realities. I am glad to see that the Parliamentary Secretary is here. I hope he will be here next week when there will be 100 fishermen representing a cross-section of the industry from British Columbia arriving in Ottawa. They will come here on Sunday and start lobbying next week. Last year some fishermen took over the offices of the Department of Fisheries in Campbell River and Alert Bay. Now they are spending
about $50,000 to come to Ottawa to plead their case. It seems that this is the only way they can get the ear of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his officials.
There are some obvious reasons the industry is dying. The habitat is a mess. Enhancement at best is minimal. There are 19 nations off our coast harvesting our salmon. In 1979, the U.S.A. harvested 99 million fish; Japon, 62 million; and B.C., 23 million. Japan alone had four mother ships which harvested 37 million salmon off our coast. That is 50 per cent more with those four mother ships than the entire Canadian catch. Much of this is taking place outside the 200-mile limit in international waters.
If the Minister says that his Department is doing such a good job, why are they not policing that? Why are they not checking the tags, and why are they not raising a ruckus out there? The total emphasis of the Department is placed upon reducing, restructuring and essentially depreciating the role of commercial fishermen. They have built hatcheries for sports fishermen; that is fine, but what about enhancement for commercial fishermen?
I ask the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary whether the Department is going to focus all its attention on a buyback program to reduce the capacity of the fleet and give almost no attention at all to habitat enhancement? The Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) is willing to assign workers from prison camps to work on enhancement. The Minister of Fisheries apparently will not accept. We need to clean up the habitat. We need to implement full scale, immediate small stream enhancement.
I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if we are going to be serious about addressing the problems of offshore fisheries? Are we going to get serious about negotiating with the United States on the salmon agreement on the Fraser River catch? Are we serious about making the Minister's advisory committee a functional group to provide input; to provide not only advice, but to listen to the advice of the industry and make it a full participant in the action which is going on out there?
It is clear from the statistics I have given that the Department is not doing its job. If up to 50 per cent of the value of the landed catch is used for administration, what is left of the value of the industry? It is no wonder that the Department focuses entirely on restricting entry when we really need to restore the fish. Why not raise production? Why not raise the stock? Why not make sure that there are more salmon out there, instead of making sure that fewer and fewer people will be able to work, and more and more people who have seen the fishing industry as a way of life losing it?

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-MANAGEMENT COSTS OF WEST COAST SALMON FISHERY. (B) NUMBER OF VESSELS ENGAGED IN COMMERCIAL SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be here to respond to the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). I know him to be a most interested and sincere member of the Fisheries Committee and a fine gentleman. But his powers of exaggeration in making a point often
January 31, 1984

leave one slightly confused, and a little bit at a loss to understand what the essential point is.
As the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) has already explained, the operating budget of the Department of the Pacific Coast covers a great deal more than just fisheries management, as implied by the Hon. Member. Moreover, the value of the resource should be based not only on the commercial fishery but also the native and sport fisheries.
The analysis put forward by the Hon. Member overstates the costs dramatically and understates the value of our programs. For example, some costly items are short or medium-term. 1 think in particular about the Salmonid Enhancement Program. I might add that I find rather amazing the statement that we are spending too much on management when part of that management cost is the Salmonid Enhancement Program. We heard that in the second minute of the seven-minute dissertation. After seven and one-half minutes, Mr. Speaker was saying, "wrap it up". Then we hear the Hon. Member saying that we really ought to be spending more on enhancement. I think the Department of Fisheries in the Pacific region has done a great job on the enchancement program. It has done a great job involving the public and working with the public in every way possible.
I want to assure the Hon. Member, as I am sure he already knows, being the gentleman that he is, that the Minister of
Adjournment Debate
Fisheries does not for one second believe that the problems of the fisheries-East Coast, West Coast, fresh water-originate with the fishermen, or that the solutions can only be found by fishermen paying the cost of those solutions. I know the Hon. Member does not believe that. I want to assure him that the fishermen from his riding, from all of that great beautiful area of the Pacific Coast and western Canada, who come to Ottawa will get a hearing. I hope they are as compassionate and as interested, but not as articulate as the Hon. Member opposite who, because his great powers of exaggeration, often leave me and many other people who are greatly interested in his concerns somewhat confused about what it is he really wants. I know that if this Hon. Member puts his mind to it, if he is interested in real progress, if he is interested in real solutions, not just in scoring political points, as important an activity as that is for a politician, he can be part of the solution, not just part of stirring up the problem. I look forward to working with him.
